solves.reasoning: ③ 'that' is wrong: 'know that it is you've achieved' needs a nominal relative pronoun with built-in antecedent. The original requires 'what': 'know what it is you've achieved'.
② 'dramatically' is wrong: modifying the noun 'conclusion' requires an adjective. 'dramatically conclusion' (adverb+noun) is wrong; should be 'dramatic conclusion'.
④ 'like' is wrong: 'you can more like convince' — needs the adverb 'likely' not the preposition/verb 'like'. 'more likely convince' is correct.
② 'telling' is wrong: 'you need telling us' — 'need' requires to-infinitive here: 'you need to tell us'. Gerund after 'need' means passive (needing to be told).
④ 'staying' is wrong: convince + object + to-infinitive structure requires 'to stay'. 'convince readers staying' is incorrect — must be 'convince readers to stay'.
③ 'forgotten' is wrong: 'what it is you've forgotten from the very beginning' makes no sense. The passage is about what you've achieved — readers know your achievement from the start.
④ 'abandon' is wrong: 'convince more readers to abandon the whole story' contradicts the purpose — the goal is to convince readers to stay, not abandon.
② 'dull' is wrong: 'no matter how dull or groundbreaking' — dull (지루한) is negative paired with positive groundbreaking, contradicting 'exciting' in the original which pairs two positives.
③ 'pick up' is wrong: 'dwindle and pick up' is contradictory — you cannot decrease and recover simultaneously. Original is 'dwindle and trail off' (both decreasing/fading).
Online readers don't have the ___ to wait for the big reveal. 'Patience' (인내심) fits perfectly — the passage explicitly says online readers lack patience for the ending.
Your ___ may still dwindle and trail off. The blank refers to your audience/readers = 'readership'. Authorship/friendship/leadership don't fit the reading context.
After 'dwindle... but ___': the silver lining is that at least the vast majority know what you've achieved from the beginning. Choice 3 directly matches this passage content.
T: Passage clearly states academic writing order: hypothesis → experiment → more testing → 'ta-da! I proved this.' This is the sequence described.
F: Presenting conclusion first doesn't cause faster dwindling — it means 'at least the vast majority know what you've achieved from the very beginning' (positive outcome).
③ is the non-match: 'online readers tend to patiently wait to the end' contradicts 'we don't have the patience to wait for your big reveal at the end'.
Passage says 'the opening line — the "hook," in journalistic terms'. The journalistic term for the opening line is 'hook'.
'you need to tell us up front' — 'up front' (2단어) means beforehand/in advance, conveying that conclusions should be revealed early.
[조건] specifies 'grab'. The passage says 'If you grab their attention early' — the blank is exactly 'grab' (1단어).
